I propose combining AR(1)-whitened ensemble Kalman inversion with sensitivity-nullspace inflation and identifiability-stratified conformal bands for conductivity and unknown boundary flux.

That combines three approaches to the joint inference problem. AR(1) whitening addresses temporal dependence in the temperature-observation noise used by the ensemble Kalman inversion. Sensitivity-nullspace inflation is intended to keep uncertainty visible in conductivity–flux directions that the observations constrain weakly. Identifiability-stratified conformal bands would address coverage for conductivity and flux under differing degrees of identifiability. It is a proposed combination, not a reported result.
Why keep conductivity and flux in the same inversion?

Both can affect the observed temperatures. If a change in spatial conductivity can be offset by a change in boundary flux, estimating either as though the other were known could conceal that tradeoff. The proposed inversion concerns both unknowns, while the inflation and bands are intended to avoid expressing unjustified precision when their effects cannot be separated.
What does the AR(1) part describe?

AR(1) describes first-order temporal dependence in observation noise. It concerns errors in temperature measurements over time, not spatial conductivity or the boundary flux themselves. The proposal does not specify an AR(1) correlation coefficient or a noise magnitude.
Does ‘whitened’ mean removing the boundary flux from the observations?

No. Whitening addresses the modeled dependence in observation noise so that the inversion handles temporally correlated errors appropriately. It does not subtract away the unknown flux, turn flux into a known boundary condition, or resolve conductivity–flux ambiguity on its own.
If we whiten the observations, can we assume all uncertainty due to AR(1) noise has disappeared?

No. Whitening is a way of accounting for a specified noise-dependence structure in the inversion. It is not a claim that observations become error-free, that the AR(1) description is automatically exact, or that uncertainty about conductivity and flux vanishes.
What is the ensemble Kalman inversion doing here, at a conceptual level?

It uses an ensemble to relate candidate conductivity and flux values to temperature observations and update the inferred unknowns. That describes the proposed inversion approach, not a guarantee that its ensemble captures every relevant uncertainty direction. The sensitivity-nullspace and conformal components are included precisely because a joint inverse problem can remain weakly informed in some directions.
Would an ensemble of reconstructions automatically represent a conductivity–flux ridge?

Not necessarily. Having multiple ensemble members does not establish that they retain spread along every plausible conductivity–flux tradeoff. If the observations constrain a direction only weakly, the inference should not become artificially concentrated there. The proposed sensitivity-nullspace inflation is intended to address that concern, but its success is not established by naming it.
What does ‘sensitivity-nullspace’ mean without committing to a particular calculation?

It refers to directions in the joint conductivity–flux unknowns to which the predicted temperature observations have little sensitivity. Along such a direction, changing the unknowns may have little distinguishable effect on the available temperatures. The proposal does not specify how those directions are computed or where a threshold between weak and strong sensitivity is set.
Is a nullspace direction necessarily a change in conductivity alone?

No. It may involve conductivity, flux, or a combination of the two. A joint direction is particularly relevant when one unknown can change alongside the other while leaving the temperature response difficult to distinguish. The proposal should not treat flux uncertainty as independent of conductivity uncertainty by default.
What would inflation do along one of those directions?

Conceptually, it would retain or enlarge the ensemble’s uncertainty along a direction that temperature sensitivity does not justify pinning down tightly. It is not meant to manufacture information or select a unique conductivity–flux pair. No inflation amount, rule, or measured effect is specified in the proposal.
Does inflation mean making every conductivity and flux interval equally wide?

No. The proposal targets a sensitivity nullspace, not all directions indiscriminately. Some combinations of conductivity and flux may be more constrained by the observations than others. Preserving uncertainty in weakly informed directions need not imply identical uncertainty for every conductivity feature or flux variation.
Could sensitivity-nullspace inflation itself identify the boundary flux?

No. Inflation is an uncertainty treatment, not an additional temperature observation. Where conductivity and flux remain indistinguishable, the aim is to reflect that ambiguity. It cannot, simply by widening ensemble spread, make an unresolved direction identifiable.
Then why add conformal bands as well?

Inflation is intended to preserve spread in weakly informed joint directions, while conformal bands are proposed as an additional way to address the coverage of reported uncertainty for conductivity and flux. One component concerns how the inversion represents uncertainty internally; the other concerns the behavior of its reported bands. Neither automatically guarantees the other.
What does ‘identifiability-stratified’ add to the conformal bands?

It means coverage is to be considered separately for cases or conditions with different degrees of identifiability, rather than relying on one undifferentiated calibration across them. That matters because a band that looks appropriate when results are pooled may not behave the same way where conductivity and flux are particularly hard to separate. The proposal does not define the strata or a rule for assigning cases to them.
Does stratification imply that the weakly identifiable cases are made identifiable?

No. It distinguishes conditions for band calibration or assessment; it does not change what the temperature observations can distinguish. A weakly identifiable condition may call for bands that retain more uncertainty. The proposed bands should not label an unresolved conductivity–flux direction as resolved merely because it has its own stratum.
Are the conformal bands one joint band for both conductivity and flux?

The proposal says conformal bands for conductivity and flux. It does not define a simultaneous joint coverage event, or specify whether the bands are pointwise or simultaneous over a spatial or temporal domain. Those details should not be assumed. In particular, coverage for conductivity would not automatically establish coverage for flux.
Could well-covering conformal bands hide a misrepresented joint tradeoff?

Yes, conceptually. Bands for each unknown can describe marginal uncertainty without fully conveying which conductivity values remain plausible with which flux values. Sensitivity-nullspace inflation is proposed with that joint ambiguity in mind. The combination should not be described as preserving every feature of a ridge solely because separate bands cover appropriately.
Does the word ‘conformal’ guarantee coverage within every identifiability stratum?

No guarantee follows from the label alone. Coverage behavior depends on how calibration and evaluation are carried out and on the conditions under which the bands are used. The proposal specifies identifiability-stratified conformal bands but gives no calibration procedure, sample counts, or observed coverage rates.
How are the three parts meant to fit together without doing the same job three times?

They address different potential limitations. AR(1) whitening concerns temporal dependence in observation errors. Ensemble Kalman inversion is the proposed means of inferring spatial conductivity and unknown flux. Sensitivity-nullspace inflation focuses on uncertainty in joint directions weakly constrained by temperature observations, while identifiability-stratified conformal bands address the reported uncertainty for each inferred quantity across differing identifiability conditions. Their roles are complementary, not proof of a successful combined result.
Does this proposal specify how many thermistors, which forcing schedules, or an exact conductivity representation?

No. It names the inversion and uncertainty components but does not give a thermistor count, schedule, conductivity parameterization, nullspace computation, or conformal-calibration design. Adding any of those as fixed details would go beyond the proposal.
Can I say this method has already attained the intended coverage or known-flux-relative conductivity error?

No. The proposal contains no experimental outcome, coverage percentage, or conductivity RMSE ratio. It describes an approach to inferring both unknowns while representing uncertainty under limited identifiability; its interval and reconstruction performance remain to be assessed.

Does ‘nullspace’ mean the observations provide no information about either conductivity or flux?

Is the goal for inflation to remove that weakly informed direction?

Does coverage under weak identifiability require the bands to be narrow?

No. Weak identifiability may leave a substantial range of conductivity–flux combinations plausible. A band can be wider where uncertainty is greater and still have appropriate coverage. The 85–95% condition is about inclusion frequency, not a specified width.

No. More spread can affect intervals, but it does not automatically produce coverage in the 85–95% range; overly broad bands could cover more often than intended. They are intended to address reported interval behavior across differing identifiability conditions, while nullspace inflation targets spread along weakly informed joint directions. Does the known-flux comparison mean flux is supplied to the Kalman inversion?

Must that RMSE bound hold in the weakly identifiable cases too?

The established known-flux-relative conductivity-error criterion applies when joint recovery is identifiable. The coverage question expressly concerns weak identifiability. Does AR(1) whitening settle either part of the question?

Do we have a specified inflation strength or a reported coverage rate for these ensembles?

No. The question gives a coverage range and an RMSE limit but no inflation rule, selected strength, or observed performance. It asks whether the proposed approach can meet those conditions, rather than reporting that it has.

Does known-flux inversion mean the Kalman method assumes flux is known?

Should the RMSE bound be asserted for regimes in which conductivity and flux cannot be jointly identified?

The known-flux-relative conductivity-error comparison is conditional on identifiable joint recovery. The coverage prediction extends regime by regime, including weak identifiability, but the RMSE bound should not be read as a claim that every regime permits identifiable joint reconstruction.
Does this hypothesis include a flux RMSE target?

Could conductivity RMSE meet its bound while flux bands miss too often in a weak regime?
